title: Improving offloading in diabetic feet: 3D-printed custom accommodative insoles outperform standard of care
content:
by Brittney C. Muir, Kimberly A. Nickerson, Christina Carranza, Mathew Sunil Varre, Avocet Nagle-Christensen, Dylan Heino, Ellen Y. Li, William R. Ledoux, Scott Telfer

Introduction

3D-printed custom accommodative insoles may offer improved plantar pressure offloading compared to standard-of-care (total contact EVA base with a 4-mm Plastazote-PORON foam top layer) insoles for individuals with diabetes. We have developed two versions of 3D-printed accommodative insoles that have patient-specific geometries as well as patient-specific stiffnesses and structural behaviors. The purpose of this study is to determine if two styles of novel 3D printed accommodative insoles (pressure-based and finite element-based), with patient-specific geometries as well as local patient-specific stiffnesses, can provide greater reductions in plantar pressures for at-risk areas of the foot without increasing pressure in the regions adjacent compared to the standard-of-care and no insole, in individuals with diabetes.

Methods

Twenty-five adults with diabetes and high plantar pressure completed walking trials under no insole, standard-of-care, pressure-based insole, and finite element-based insole conditions. Peak plantar pressure and pressure-time integral were measured in high-risk regions of interest and adjacent regions. Participant comfort and preference were recorded.

Results

All insoles significantly reduced peak plantar pressure and pressure-time integral by greater than 14% in the regions of interest compared to no insole (p < 0.001). Compared with the standard-of-care, pressure-based insole and finite element-based insole further reduced peak pressure (22% and 24%, respectively) and pressure-time integral (19% and 35%, respectively) in the region of interest (p < 0.001). Finite element-based insole reduced pressure-time integral and peak plantar pressure in adjacent regions (p < 0.01), indicating broader offloading. Participant preferences and feedback indicated improvements in fit and comfort are needed across all insoles before clinical implementation.

Conclusion

There is potential for personalized, 3D-printed custom accommodative insoles as a patient-centered approach to offloading plantar pressure in individuals with diabetes. These technologies may support more effective and tailored strategies in preventing diabetic foot complications.
